high_priority_articles.summary: Thailand welcomes US-Myanmar engagement, expects ASEAN talks on country's future  Yahoo News Singapore
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira
LISBON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Thailand welcomes US engagement with Myanmar and expects discussions at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' November summit in Manila on how to proceed with the member barred since the 2021 coup, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Reuters on Friday.
The United States and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo two weeks ago, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after the coup.
"We don't want to see Myanmar isolated, we don't want Myanmar to be an arena for geopolitical rivalry ... so the US engagement is something that we welcome," he said.
Engagement "does not mean legitimizing the regime," but aims to encourage peaceful conflict resolution and reconciliation with the opposition, Sihasak, who is also deputy prime minister, added.
He said there was "some shift in ASEAN's position," citing Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing's recent visits to Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia, but said it was unclear whether the Manila summit would address restoring Myanmar's full representation.
"It's good that we're going to have a very substantive, very extensive, and very in-depth discussion on how to proceed on Myanmar," he said.
He also said Thailand and Cambodia could resolve their longstanding land and maritime boundary disputes within 12 to 18 months despite limited progress.
"It is possible, everything is possible," he said, cautioning that confidence-building and addressing security concerns along the land border, where clashes have occurred, must come first.
Cambodia launched a conciliation process under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea in June to resolve the maritime boundary dispute, after Thailand terminated a 2001 joint development framework in May following deadly border clashes. The first meeting was held about a month ago.
"Right now, we haven't achieved, to be very frank, much progress," he said.
The maritime dispute centers on overlapping claims to about 26,000 sq km in the Gulf of Thailand, believed to hold oil and gas reserves worth around $300 billion. Thailand wants the boundary defined before discussing resource-sharing, he said.
Thailand-EU free-trade talks are in their final stage and could conclude by year-end if there is mutual political will, he added.
(Reporting by Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira in Lisbon; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

high_priority_articles.summary: Trump eases tariffs on Canadian imports weeks before US midterms, offering relief to Maine  The Times of IndiaUS lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods before midterm elections  BBCTrump lifts some Canada tariffs ahead of midterms  The HinduTrump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as Senator Collins faces close race  ReutersUS expected to lift 50% tariffs on select Canadian agricultural imports, WSJ says  Investing.com India
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has eased some tariffs on Canadian imports, with the move coming just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections. The decision could benefit Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is facing a tough re-election contest in Maine, a state whose economy has been affected by the trade dispute with Canada.
The White House said the changes would remove tariffs on certain products, including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment". However, the administration will also introduce tariffs on other goods, including carpets, certain valves and waste products. The new measures will take effect on October 30.
Collins said she had "secured" the exemptions for products important to Maine's agricultural sector, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
Collins seeks relief for Maine businesses
Collins, who faces a strong challenge from a Democratic candidate, said farmers in her state depend on supplies from Canada that are difficult or expensive to source elsewhere.
She said many farmers "rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."
The senator's intervention comes as Democrats target her seat in their bid to take control of Congress from Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections. 
Maine shares a border with Canada, and businesses in the state have felt the effects of Trump's trade policies.
The partial tariff relief could ease costs for some businesses, although the introduction of duties on other Canadian products means the changes will not benefit every sector.

Trade tensions strain US-Canada ties
The United States and Canada have closely connected economies, with roughly 70 per cent of Canadian exports going to the US. Trade relations have deteriorated since negotiations between the two countries broke down in August, prompting Trump to impose a fresh round of tariffs.
Earlier US duties on Canadian cars, steel, aluminium and lumber have hurt businesses, contributed to job losses and weighed on economic growth. Canada entered a technical recession this year after its economy contracted for two consecutive quarters.
The tariffs imposed after the collapse of trade talks affected goods worth around $20 billion, equivalent to 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the US. The targeted products ranged from hockey sticks to cement.
Since returning to office for his second term, Trump has imposed extensive tariffs on imports from both allies and rivals, arguing that other countries have taken advantage of the United States.
His administration has also linked some threatened tariffs to broader political and foreign policy goals.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
A US peace proposal would ‘offer’ Ukraine European Union membership and an investment package in exchange for abandoning its bid to join NATO, The Economist reported on Thursday, Oct. 22.
The reported outline also includes a demilitarized zone in Donbas, the eastern Ukrainian region comprising Donetsk and Luhansk.
Russia could receive commercial agreements with American companies, sanctions relief and restored political ties with Washington. The package also envisages resuming Russian gas supplies to Europe, including reviving Nord Stream, according to the report.
Ukrainian officials are familiar with the general framework but have not received full details of the latest US proposals, The Economist reported. Neither Kyiv nor Washington has announced that Ukraine has accepted the terms.
One Ukrainian official told the magazine that Kyiv fears US representatives could pursue lucrative deals with Moscow before the war ends, allowing Russia to gain economic and diplomatic benefits while fighting continues.
Kyiv seeks enforceable security guarantees
The reported outline follows talks in Oslo on Oct. 20 between President Volodymyr Zelensky, US envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders. The discussions covered Ukraine’s security, territorial questions, sanctions and postwar economic prospects.
US officials described work on two tracks: Ukraine’s sovereignty, security guarantees, European integration and reconstruction; and a separate framework addressing Russia and future security arrangements.
Witkoff subsequently met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
After that meeting, Zelensky said Washington had relayed that Moscow was open to resuming trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US. He said the teams could meet by early November, although no date had been set.
The Kremlin then indicated that Putin was ready in principle to resume talks around mid-November.
Kyiv is pressing for security commitments it considers enforceable. Zelensky has said Ukraine is negotiating US guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5 and backed by a vote in Congress.
He described NATO membership, bilateral US guarantees and a European-led Coalition of the Willing as complementary parts of Ukraine’s security framework. No final agreement on those guarantees has been announced.
Washington cannot grant EU membership
The reported offer does not establish an agreed accession date or mean Ukraine would automatically join the EU.
Under the EU’s accession rules, membership requires negotiations, the European Parliament’s consent, unanimous approval by the Council and ratification of an accession treaty by all member states and the candidate country.
A previous US-backed peace framework reportedly proposed that Ukraine could join the EU as soon as January 2027. Kyiv Post reported in December 2025 that the proposal would involve territorial concessions and require Brussels to consider changes to its enlargement process. That was a proposed timetable, not an agreed accession date.
Renewed Russian energy supplies would also require European decisions. The EU adopted a legally binding phaseout of Russian gas imports in January, with remaining long-term LNG supplies due to end from January 2027 and pipeline supplies from autumn 2027.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, Germany’s government opposes reopening Nord Stream, which also faces US and EU sanctions.
The reported package therefore includes benefits Washington cannot deliver alone. Ukraine’s accession and any lasting return of Russian gas to the EU market would require agreement in Europe, alongside a settlement accepted by Kyiv and Moscow.

Piyush Goyal warned that Europe’s carbon border mechanism and high steel import duties could increase living costs and hurt industries. He projected India-Germany trade could reach €310 billion, while highlighting the proposed India-EU FTA and cooperation in strategic sectors
New Delhi: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has warned European countries that the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and high import duties on steel could raise cost of living, make industries uncompetitive and hurt consumers.
During a question and answer session at the Berlin Global Dialogue 2026, the minister said, “If you have put a CBAM on yourself, you put a 50 per cent import duty to bring steel into your country, you are inviting disaster. He noted that trust is the hardest currency in commerce today. “Your cost of living will go up. Your people will be unhappy. Your industry will be out priced,” Goyal added.
Speaking at another programme in Berlin, the minister noted that India-Germany bilateral trade could rise to €310 billion from around €31 billion at present if the two countries focus on complementary strengths and jointly create products and technologies. However, he did not specify a timeline for achieving the target.
Notably, Goyal is on an official visit to Germany and the Netherlands from October 22 to 27 and was accompanied by a delegation of about 100 Indian businesses and startups. Meanwhile, German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Katherina Reiche called for reducing red tape on both sides and undertaking joint projects, saying bilateral trade could be doubled.
Addressing the India-Germany Business Roundtable and inaugurating the India Centre of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), Goyal said the India-EU free trade agreement (FTA) is expected to be signed by the end of this year and could become operational within the next four to five months.
Apart from that, Goyal and Reiche held a bilateral meeting earlier in the day and discussed cooperation in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, energy and other sectors. “Discussed opportunities in AI, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, green hydrogen, renewable energy, energy storage, and resilient supply chains, as well as increased investment in India’s industrial and digital ecosystems,” Goyal said in a social media post.
“We also exchanged views on how the India-EU FTA will prove to be a game-changer that would help businesses in both India and Germany realise their full potential,” he added.

Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – Japanese Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is strengthening Vietnam’s manufacturing capacity and accelerating the green transition, as more Japanese companies expand production and adopt sustainable industrial solutions. 
Vietnam has become an important market and strategic manufacturing base in Southeast Asia for Japanese investors, reflecting their long-term confidence in the country’s economic potential and sustainable growth prospects. 
Investment cooperation has been a key pillar of Vietnam-Japan economic ties. According to the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Japan has more than 5,800 active investment projects in Vietnam, with total registered capital exceeding 81 billion USD. 
Free trade agreements (FTAs) have also created favourable conditions for businesses in both countries through tariff reductions, rules of origin, and trade facilitation, opening up opportunities for deeper participation in regional production networks and supply chains. 
Major Japanese companies, including Honda, Panasonic, Kao Vietnam and Sumitomo, have maintained and expanded their operations in Vietnam. Meanwhile, new Japanese investment is flowing into industrial parks, supporting greener manufacturing and the adoption of more sustainable production solutions. 
A recent example is Japanese group Oji’s launch of construction of a new aseptic carton packaging factory under its Oji Liquid Pak (OLP) brand. The project, with an investment of 110 million USD, is located in Long Thanh High-Tech Park in Dong Nai province. 
The investment demonstrates Oji Liquid Pak’s long-term commitment to Vietnam and reinforces the country’s role as a strategic manufacturing and supply hub for the group in Southeast Asia. It is also expected to support the region’s shift towards circular packaging solutions that meet evolving policy requirements. 
Nguyen Quoc An, deputy head of the Dong Nai Industrial and Economic Zones Authority (DNIEZA), said large-scale projects like this would contribute to local industrial development, strengthen domestic production capacity and help Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in regional supply chains.

Tran Viet Ha, Deputy Head of the Ho Chi Minh City Export Processing and Industrial Zones Authority (HEPZA), said the authority was working to help investors start projects sooner after registration and reduce procedures related to planning and construction. 
HEPZA aims to resolve matters within its authority directly and coordinate with other agencies on issues requiring inter-agency cooperation. It is also shifting from a focus on administrative procedures to monitoring projects throughout their life cycle, from investment preparation to operation.

The resolution shifts Vietnam’s investment attraction strategy towards quality rather than quantity, prioritising high technology, innovation, workforce development and technology transfer.

high_priority_articles.summary: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran  The GuardianIstanbul meeting: A new division of labor in the Iran war?  Iran InternationalEuropean, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks  Al JazeeraTurkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way  ReutersEgypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan say 'Israeli occupation main source of regional instability'  The Times of Israel
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and the Bank of Thailand (BOT) have joined the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) BLOOM initiative as policymaker members.
The three central banks will work with industry players to develop common approaches for accepting, exchanging and settling digital money across borders.
Launched in October 2025, BLOOM (Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency) brings together policymakers, financial institutions, payment networks and technology providers.
It supports settlement involving tokenised bank liabilities and regulated stablecoins.
Visa, Mastercard and Ripple among new participants
MAS also announced that Airwallex, Mastercard, Maybank, Monee, Nium, Ripple, ShopeePay, Visa and the World Bank Group have joined the initiative.
Participants are developing digital money applications across payments, treasury and trade finance.
The World Bank Group will contribute its experience in payment systems modernisation, cross-border payments and financial inclusion.
Three areas of cooperation
BLOOM will focus on three areas: cross-border acceptance and settlement, interoperability between digital money systems, and programmable controls. These controls include identity verification and sanctions screening.
MAS said common implementation frameworks would reduce the need for separate arrangements with counterparties or markets. This would lower implementation costs and shorten time to market.
Leong Sing Chiong, Deputy Managing Director (Markets and Development), MAS, said,
“To fully harness the benefits of using digital money, collaboration among policymakers and industry participants will be needed to address practical issues around acceptance, settlement and interoperability.”
Aznan bin Abdul Aziz, Deputy Governor, BNM, said,
“A future where frictionless cross-border payments can be made using multiple digital monies is now closer to a tangible reality than a far-fetched fantasy. BNM looks forward to exploring such a future through the BLOOM initiative with all participating central banks and industry partners.”
BLOOM builds on Project Orchid, an earlier MAS initiative that explored a digital Singapore dollar and its supporting infrastructure.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Overview and Implications of the Tariff Dispute
By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Oct 23 (Reuters) - India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters.
Background: Negotiations and Agreement Details
Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over 10 years.
The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact. Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect.
Investigation and Industry Response
India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate.
In a letter to the commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India (ISWAI) wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom."
"The preferential tariff treatment negotiated ... could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.
ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond.
Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment, and Diageo did not respond to a request for comment. Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation.
Big Implications for India's Drinks Sector
Impact on Foreign Investors
Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back-tax. Such disputes have embroiled the likes of Samsung and Volkswagen.
Pernod's Ongoing Legal Challenges
Pernod is already facing antitrust cases in India and a $314 million back-tax demand from Indian authorities, who accuse it of undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing.
Market Impact and Industry Concerns
ISWAI's letter underscores the shockwaves the investigation has sent through India's $65 billion alcohol market. Britain accounts for almost 75% of India's imported spirits, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, according to Crisil Ratings.
Indian government inspectors have told companies that they do not benefit from the reduced 75% tariff on bulk imports of Scotch concentrates, which must be declared under a customs classification that attracts a 150% duty, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Pernod and Diageo import bulk concentrates, mixing them with other ingredients to produce hugely popular Indian brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s.
Calls for Clarification and Resolution
The three people said companies including Diageo and Pernod believe concentrates imported from Britain should benefit from the new, lower tariff. And ISWAI said in its letter that the India–UK agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant tariff lines.
An urgent clarification could ensure market-access benefits negotiated by India and Britain are realised "while avoiding uncertainty and disruption for legitimate industry participants," the letter said.
Official Responses and Next Steps
A spokesperson for the British government said: "We are working with the Government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal."
(Reporting by Aditya Kalra; Additional reporting by Shivangi Acharya and Alistair Smout; Editing by Joe Bavier)

Warsh’s First FOMC: Hawkish Dot Plot Reshapes the 2026 Rate Outlook
Warsh effectively ended “forward guidance,” emphasizing productivity and letting markets work. The shift moves away from letting the SEP, dot plot and Fed guidance define market expectations and shape the supposed natural flow of markets.
According to Hyblock CEO Shubh Varma:
 “Warsh is signaling that he wants a leaner and more forward-looking Fed. One that’s less focused on managing expectations every quarter the way Powell did, and more focused on actually modernizing how the institution works. On that broad point, they said that most serious people agree this is a good direction. There’s a view that the Fed clearly needs updating for the economy we have today.”
Counter to crypto traders’ expectations, the updated SEP shows that nine of the 19 Fed policymakers now project at least one 25-basis-point rate hike before year-end 2026. Six of those nine project two hikes. That marks a notable shift from the March dot plot, which had pointed toward one cut for the remainder of the year. Markets read the meeting as a regime shift. Bitcoin dropped below $63,000, the S&P 500 fell 1.21% on June 17, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.34%, and the 10-year Treasury yield moved to 4.49%.
Bitcoin Risks New 2026 Lows, But Positive Crypto Developments Continue
Spot Bitcoin ETF flow data. Source: CoinMarketCap
CLARITY Act Delayed, But Does It Matter Anyway?
What is clear is that the crypto market has taken the view of “if it happens, it happens.” With the emergence of new narratives, does Clarity becoming law as fast as possible even matter for trader positioning?
Hyperliquid’s performance as a decentralized exchange stands as a perfect example of this. Its ties to TradFi, including recent talks with Nasdaq, show how quickly the market is moving. So do the huge trading volumes seen in its oil futures, tokenized stocks, pre-IPO futures and SpaceX perpetual futures. Together, they demonstrate a broader pattern of innovators, Big Tech and Wall Street moving steps ahead of policymakers.
Hyperliquid’s move-fast-and-break-things style is moving financial infrastructure forward, demonstrating the validity of its use case — and in some ways, forcing the hand of US lawmakers.
Is It Time For A Sector Rotation?
A handful of fund managers agree that Bitcoin is discounted but acknowledge that investors are riding outperformers in AI and energy stocks as a better trade. This is leading to a passive or hands-off approach to BTC. Its recent drop to $59,000 was accompanied by $4.4 billion in ETF outflows, making them net negative year-to-date.
Beyond Strategy propping up the market with future multi-billion dollar buys, markets need to see ETF flows turn positive for a sustained period of time before Bitcoin and other majors react positively.
What’s On The Radar?
Currently, there are a lot of moving parts to keep up with and they’ll continue to impact crypto pricing. A more enlightening way of forecasting a way forward is to consider the following:
- What impact will the US MoU with Iran have on oil prices and energy prices down the line? Will falling oil prices poke a hole in expanding inflation?
- Will the AI buildout, wild energy markets and a euphoric IPO season continue to dominate investor mindshare and capital flows? Or will investor interest shift in Q3, Q4?
- WIll Warsh hike in Q3 or Q4?
Beyond those scenarios, crypto prices will likely depend on spot Bitcoin ETF demand, assets in newly launched Bitcoin income ETFs, Strategy’s buying and moves by other corporate digital asset treasuries.

high_priority_articles.title: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand? - Euronews
high_priority_articles.summary: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand?  Euronews
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates next week as France's bond sell-off tightens borrowing conditions across the eurozone, while ECB President Christine Lagarde has made clear that the first steps to tackle French debt woes must come from Paris, not Frankfurt.
When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.
The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.
On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.
Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.
Ratings agency Moody's, which rates France Aa3, its fourth-highest grade, with a negative outlook, delivers its verdict on Friday evening, and a downgrade is widely expected. A one-notch cut to A1 would put France's rating at the equivalent level to those assigned by S&P and Fitch.
Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.
More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.
French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".
Bonds doing the ECB's job
The case for another rate hike is still there.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.
Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday.
"For France, it’s closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".
Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.
ECB President Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament on 28 September that long-term rates "have risen notably, which will slow growth".
Could the ECB intervene?
ECB officials have played down the possibility of intervening to lower France's borrowing costs, but have stopped short of ruling it out.
The central bank bought government bonds during the eurozone debt crisis to stabilise markets and ensure its rate decisions continued to feed through to the economy.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok last week, Lagarde said that "there are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point."
"The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," the ECB president added.
Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin went further last Friday, saying the conditions for ECB intervention were not met at that time because there was no financial fragmentation in the eurozone.
However, both officials spoke before France’s 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5%.
If the ECB decides to intervene in the French bond market, one option could be the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which was created in 2022 and has never been used.
The TPI lets the ECB buy the debt of countries whose borrowing costs climb in ways it judges unjustified by their economic fundamentals and threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the eurozone.
For a country to be eligible, it needs to meet several criteria, including following EU fiscal rules and keeping its debt on a sustainable path.
France is nursing a debt-to-GDP ratio of 119.1%, and the current budget negotiations offer little prospect of a quick reduction in the deficit, which is necessary to put the debt on a sustainable path.
Meanwhile, the government expects its debt-servicing costs to rise by more than €10 billion in 2027 compared with this year.
"The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high," Brzeski wrote in a separate investor note last week.
He added that, for France, that would at least mean passing its full budget. Acting too early could be "interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules," he warned.
The ECB's other emergency tool, Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT), was created in 2012 at the height of the eurozone debt crisis to allow unlimited purchases of a struggling country's short-term bonds.
However, it is only available to governments that first sign up to a bailout programme from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism.
Instead, Brzeski expects the ECB to quietly pause the reduction of its bond holdings, reinvesting maturing debt flexibly as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Should turmoil spread to other eurozone bond markets, Brzeski sees TPI as a last resort. If France continued to fall short of EU fiscal rules, "the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France," he said.
For now, Brzeski sees next week’s rate meeting as "uneventful on action but clearly not on words".

high_priority_articles.title: Talking Point: NVIDIA’s JUPITER breakthrough brings practical quantum computing a step closer - Intelligent CIO
high_priority_articles.summary: Talking Point: NVIDIA’s JUPITER breakthrough brings practical quantum computing a step closer  Intelligent CIO
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Quantum computing is entering an exciting new phase as researchers make measurable progress towards overcoming challenges that have constrained its potential in medicine, finance and materials science.
NVIDIA’s latest experiment at Germany’s Jülich Supercomputing Centre suggests practical quantum computing is becoming more achievable.
Using JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer, NVIDIA researchers simulated a 104-qubit fault-tolerant quantum processor under realistic noise conditions. NVIDIA calls it the largest comprehensive simulation of its kind. The work also tested ‘magic-state cultivation’, a technique designed to significantly reduce the hardware requirements associated with correcting quantum errors.
NVIDIA says the approach requires 90% fewer physical qubits than previous methods. If these efficiency gains can be reproduced in physical quantum systems, they could advance commercially viable quantum computing.
Quantum error correction remains one of the industry’s most demanding technical challenges. Qubits are sensitive to environmental disturbances, making reliable calculations difficult. Fault tolerance addresses this problem by introducing resources that protect quantum information and enable dependable operations.
Reducing those requirements could improve the economics of quantum computing. Smaller systems, lower costs and more efficient architectures would make the technology increasingly accessible to researchers, businesses and industrial users.
The experiment shows how simulation can accelerate progress before hardware is constructed.
NVIDIA initially developed and tested its simulation techniques on GB200 infrastructure before scaling them to 8,192 GPUs on JUPITER. Its cuQuantum software and CUDA-Q platform supported the calculations. According to the company, development work helped reduce simulation times from weeks to days.
This acceleration matters because quantum computing development depends on testing complex architectures, identifying potential failures and refining designs. The ability to conduct these experiments more efficiently could shorten development cycles and help researchers concentrate resources on the most promising approaches.
It also highlights a productive relationship between classical and quantum computing.
Rather than competing technologies, high-performance computing and quantum systems are becoming complementary components of future computational infrastructure. Classical supercomputers can support quantum processor design, error correction research and the eventual operation of sophisticated quantum machines.
Europe has reason to welcome the breakthrough. JUPITER demonstrates the strategic value of investing in public research infrastructure. By providing the computational capacity required for pioneering quantum research, the Jülich Supercomputing Centre is strengthening Europe’s position within a competitive international technology landscape.
This illustrates how European infrastructure and American technology expertise can combine to advance scientific discovery.
Challenges remain. Researchers must validate simulation results experimentally and demonstrate that theoretical efficiency gains translate into reliable hardware operating at commercially meaningful scale.
The direction of progress is encouraging. The significance of NVIDIA’s achievement lies not simply in the number of simulated qubits but in its contribution to solving the practical problems that have delayed quantum computing’s development.
By reducing resource requirements, accelerating research and improving the understanding of fault-tolerant architectures, advances such as this could help transform quantum computing from an emerging scientific capability into a powerful industrial technology.
JUPITER has demonstrated that the journey towards useful quantum computing is gaining momentum. The next challenge is translating that momentum into working machines.

The Ripple BLOOM Initiative has garnered some traction as Singapore extends its cross-border payment initiative with the inclusion of the central banks of Malaysia and Thailand from October 23, 2026.
Table of Contents
Headed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), this initiative seeks to enhance international payments through the use of regulated stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits.
This development introduces more regional policymakers into the discourse surrounding digital currency standards and payment facilitation in Southeast Asia. Meanwhile, Cross River is incorporating Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin based on the XRP ledger into its banking core system.

What Is the Ripple BLOOM Initiative?
Ripple BLOOM Initiative is a growing topic of debate on Ripple’s stablecoin innovations and Singapore’s BLOOM project that addresses cross-border payment improvements. BLOOM stands for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency and is being spearheaded by MAS in partnership with the private sector.
MAS initiated the BLOOM project on October 16, 2025, in order to investigate how banks can leverage blockchain-enabled money in the process of international settlement. This project involves two types of digital money: tokenized bank liabilities and regulated stablecoins.
Tokenized bank liabilities are essentially tokenized bank deposits, whereas stablecoins are tokens whose aim is to hold stable value relative to some currency like the US dollar.
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative is related to general digital payment advancements, but the Singapore BLOOM project and Ripple RLUSD initiative are entirely different projects with separate objectives.
Malaysia and Thailand Join Singapore’s BLOOM Initiative
BNM and BOT became members of BLOOM among policymakers on October 23, 2026. This means that both central banks will have an opportunity to influence the development of the standards for digital currency and international transactions.
This project includes several organizations from the private sector, including Circle (stablecoin issuer), DBS (Singapore bank), Stripe (payments provider), and the World Bank Group.
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative is connected with the broader topic of digital payments because of the growing importance of stablecoins as instruments for interbank payments. However, Malaysia and Thailand became participants in Singapore’s BLOOM project.
BLOOM focuses mostly on wholesale finance activities and not retail payment transactions. This is done through trade finance and corporate treasury management, where companies require transfers of huge amounts of money across national borders.
Through the establishment of common standards, participating entities hope to cut down costs of payments, streamline the settlement process, and avoid country-specific arrangements.
How the Ripple BLOOM Initiative Relates to Stablecoin Payments
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative would serve as a good keyword for analyzing the trend towards blockchain-based payments despite BLOOM being an initiative by MAS. The goal of this project is to enhance cross-border payments by streamlining the transfer and settlement of digital currencies and deposits.
One of the main focus areas of the BLOOM Initiative is programmable compliance. It involves incorporating rules like sanctions screening and limits on transfers into the payment process.
BLOOM is also looking into ways to distribute the settlement assets, the possibility of having multiple currencies, and connecting various payment networks. The establishment of risk management standards is another one of BLOOM’s objectives.
In case these attempts prove successful, businesses will be able to transfer funds between the participating markets with ease. But this depends on how the standards are developed and implemented.
BLOOM by Ripple Initiative does not constitute a partnership or payment network by Ripple. Malaysia and Thailand will participate in shaping the standards for BLOOM, but cross-border stablecoin offerings have not yet been introduced.
BLOOM Builds on Singapore’s Project Orchid
The BLOOM project of Singapore extends the scope of the earlier Project Orchid initiated by MAS in 2021 for studying the digital version of the Singapore dollar.
The Ripple BLOOM Initiative discussion represents yet another attempt to bridge blockchain and traditional finance. The involvement of Malaysia and Thailand can lead to more collaboration within the region, yet the results depend on further actions.
Cross River Integrates Ripple’s RLUSD on the XRP Ledger
Cross River is implementing the USD-denominated RLUSD stablecoin from Ripple on the XRP Ledger within the bank’s core banking framework. This implementation is aimed at facilitating real-time settlement, cross-border payments, and 24/7 treasury transactions via one API.
This development connects to the larger topic of the Ripple BLOOM Initiative in the context of digital payments, although they are different initiatives. The BLOOM project is attempting to create common standards for cross-border payments. This initiative’s success will be dependent on regional cooperation, regulation, and adoption.

BLOOM expands across borders
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said Bank Negara Malaysia and the Bank of Thailand joined Singapore's BLOOM cross-border digital money initiative as policymaker members on Friday. BLOOM, short for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency, was launched in October last year and the three central banks will work with industry players on common approaches for accepting, exchanging and settling digital money across institutions, networks and borders. BLOOM covers tokenised deposits, regulated stablecoins and settlement across payment networks, with a focus on interoperability and programmable controls.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said shared frameworks would lower implementation costs and shorten time to market, while the authority said the three central banks would look at how international standards and jurisdiction-specific supervisory expectations can be applied to such transactions. What the central banks will do
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the three central banks will center their work on three areas: acceptance and settlement across jurisdictions, interoperability between digital money arrangements, and programmable controls such as identity verification, sanctions screening and transaction controls. Bank Negara Malaysia separately outlined three pilot schemes, announced in February, to test a ringgit stablecoin and tokenised deposits for domestic and cross-border wholesale payments in 2026.
The Bank of Thailand's move aligns with a broader push among Southeast Asian monetary authorities to adopt distributed ledger technology, and the authority has not set a timeline for the common frameworks or said when the first cross-border transactions under the expanded membership would be processed. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said central bank involvement is meant to ensure public policy and regulatory considerations are built in as those approaches take shape.
Participants and potential impact
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said BLOOM's industry roster has grown beyond its founding group of Singapore lenders DBS, OCBC and UOB, along with Standard Chartered, JPMorgan Chase, Coinbase, StraitsX, Circle and Temasek. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the initiative brings together policymakers, banks, payment networks and technology providers to push digital money into cross-border financial activity, and it said the World Bank Group's presence is expected to bring global experience in payment-system modernization, cross-border payments and financial inclusion. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said BLOOM builds on Project Orchid, a 2021 MAS effort to explore uses for a digital Singapore dollar, and the current phase focuses on the technical and policy plumbing needed for next-generation payments infrastructure.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said the arrangement could eventually mean fewer bilateral integrations and a more uniform set of compliance expectations when moving tokenised value between markets. The Monetary Authority of Singapore said shared implementation frameworks and aligned commercial and operating arrangements would cut the need for financial institutions to strike separate deals with every counterparty or market, lowering implementation costs and shortening time to market.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Malaysia and Thailand are joining Singapore to make cross-border digital payments work more smoothly, bringing three central banks together to develop common rules for regulated stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits.
The move could help financial institutions transfer and settle digital money across borders with fewer delays and lower implementation costs.
Malaysia and Thailand Join Singapore’s Stablecoin Push
On October 23, 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced that Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and the Bank of Thailand (BOT) had joined its BLOOM initiative as policymaker members.
BLOOM, which stands for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency, was launched in October 2025. It brings policymakers and financial firms together to develop ways to use digital money across different countries and payment networks.
With Malaysia and Thailand joining, the three central banks will work with industry participants to establish common approaches for accepting, exchanging and settling regulated stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits across borders.
Three Countries Target Easier Digital Payments
The partnership focuses on a major challenge for cross-border payments: different countries and financial institutions may use separate systems and rules to process digital money.
BLOOM will examine how transactions can be settled between institutions and markets, and how different digital money networks can work together. The initiative also aims to reduce the need for banks and payment firms to establish separate arrangements with every counterparty in each market.
This could lower implementation costs and help financial institutions introduce cross-border payment services faster. However, the announcement does not confirm an immediate launch of a shared stablecoin payment service.
Stablecoin Transfers to Include Safety Checks
The three central banks will also work with industry participants on safeguards such as identity verification, sanctions screening and transaction controls. The aim is to support cross-border digital money transfers while accounting for international standards and each country’s regulatory requirements.
Bank Negara Malaysia Deputy Governor Aznan bin Abdul Aziz said payments using multiple forms of digital money were moving closer to reality.“The world of payments progresses rapidly,” he said, adding that BNM looked forward to exploring frictionless cross-border payments through BLOOM with other central banks and industry partners.
For Malaysia and Thailand, joining the initiative creates a path to help shape how regulated stablecoins and tokenized deposits could be used across borders. The next step is developing common frameworks for settlement and interoperability, rather than launching a new digital currency.

high_priority_articles.summary: India’s liquor trade group asks government to clarify Scotch tariffs under U.K. trade deal  Vinetur
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Investigators told importers that bulk Scotch concentrates may still face a 150% duty, alarming Pernod Ricard and Diageo
Friday, October 23, 2026
A trade group representing major liquor companies in India has asked the government for urgent intervention after Indian investigators told importers that reduced tariffs under the new India-United Kingdom trade deal do not apply to bulk shipments of Scotch whisky concentrates, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.
The dispute centers on one of the most closely watched parts of the trade agreement, which took effect on July 15 after years of negotiations. Under the pact, India agreed to cut import duties on certain Scotch whisky products from 150% to 75% immediately, with the rate set to fall to 40% over 10 years. The British government had said the deal would help flagship U.K. products such as whisky.
But Indian tax investigators have privately told companies that bulk imports of Scotch whisky concentrate should not receive the lower 75% duty and instead must be classified under a customs category that attracts the full 150% tariff, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters. That position has raised the first major dispute over implementation of the free trade deal and has alarmed companies that rely on imported Scotch spirit for products made and sold in India.
In a letter sent on Friday to India’s commerce minister, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India said the classification issue threatens to undermine a key market access benefit that India and Britain negotiated and agreed under the pact. The group said the preferential tariff treatment could effectively become unavailable for those imports if the current interpretation is maintained.
The association did not comment on the contents of the letter. India’s commerce ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The issue has become more sensitive after India’s Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod Ricard and Diageo this month and questioned executives as part of an investigation into whether the companies wrongly classified imported products in order to claim the lower tariff rate. Earlier this week, both companies told Reuters they were cooperating with Indian authorities.
Pernod declined to comment further. Diageo did not respond to a request for comment.
The case matters because India is one of the world’s largest alcoholic drinks markets and a crucial growth engine for global spirits companies. The country’s liquor market is worth about $65 billion, and imported spirits remain a small but influential part of the business. According to Crisil Ratings, Britain accounts for nearly 75% of spirits imported into India, driven mainly by Scotch whisky.
For companies such as Pernod and Diageo, the tariff interpretation has commercial importance beyond imported premium bottles sold directly to consumers. Both groups import bulk Scotch concentrates and use them in India to make widely sold brands including Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s. Industry executives say the economics of those products depend heavily on whether the imported spirit qualifies for the lower duty.
People familiar with the matter said the companies believe the goods shipped from the U.K. should fall under the tariff lines covered by the trade agreement and should therefore receive the reduced 75% duty. The industry association made the same argument in its letter, saying the agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant customs lines.
The group also warned that uncertainty over classification is already affecting business planning and could disrupt legitimate industry operations unless the government issues a clarification quickly. It said prompt action would help ensure that the market access gains negotiated by India and Britain are actually delivered in practice.
A spokesperson for the British government said London is working with New Delhi to resolve the issue and to make sure British companies can export under the tariff terms set out in the trade deal.
The disagreement comes against a broader backdrop of tension between foreign companies and Indian authorities over import classifications and tax demands. Such disputes have long been a source of concern for overseas investors in India, who have in past years faced large claims for back taxes and penalties. Multinational companies including Samsung and Volkswagen have also been caught in customs and tax fights with the Indian government.
Pernod in particular is already under pressure in India on several fronts. The company, whose largest market by volume is India, is facing antitrust cases and a $314 million tax claim from Indian authorities, who have accused it of undervaluing some imports. Pernod has denied any wrongdoing.
The tariff fight over Scotch is politically sensitive as well because whisky was one of the most difficult issues during the India-U.K. trade talks. India has long maintained some of the highest import duties in the world on alcoholic beverages, and Scotch producers had pressed hard for cuts to improve access to a market with rising incomes and strong demand for premium spirits. The final deal was presented by both governments as a breakthrough, with lower tariffs seen as a concrete commercial win for British exporters.
The current dispute suggests that even after a trade agreement takes effect, the commercial outcome can depend on how customs authorities interpret product categories at the border. In this case, the disagreement is not over whether tariff cuts were negotiated, but over which forms of Scotch whisky are entitled to benefit from them.
That question is especially important for India’s domestic spirits industry because bulk Scotch imports are used as inputs in blended products made inside the country. If those imports remain subject to 150% duties, companies may face higher costs, altered sourcing decisions and pressure on margins in a market where competition is intense. Industry officials say it could also weaken one of the practical benefits that the trade agreement was expected to deliver.
So far, Indian authorities have not publicly explained why bulk Scotch concentrate should be excluded from the lower tariff bracket, and there has been no official clarification from the government on how the relevant customs lines should be interpreted under the trade pact. Until that changes, producers and importers are left facing uncertainty over both future shipments and the potential tax exposure tied to past imports now under investigation.
For Pernod and Diageo, the matter carries both legal and financial risk. Investigators are examining whether the companies’ use of the lower rate was proper, and the answer could determine whether they face additional duty demands. For the wider industry, the case has become a test of whether one of the headline promises of the India-U.K. agreement will hold once it reaches the customs gate.

high_priority_articles.title: QatarEnergy Signs Long-Term Deal to Buy U.S. LNG as Iran War Disrupts Exports - gCaptain
high_priority_articles.summary: QatarEnergy Signs Long-Term Deal to Buy U.S. LNG as Iran War Disrupts Exports  gCaptain
high_priority_articles.full_text:
QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran.
The agreements, announced Thursday, cover 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) each from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054.
Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. terminals. Pricing will be linked to the Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee.
The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March.
The attacks damaged two LNG production trains with a combined capacity of 12.8 MTPA, knocking out approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia.
While the U.S. contracts will not begin delivering cargoes until the early 2030s, they will give QatarEnergy an additional source of supply outside the Persian Gulf, where energy infrastructure and shipping have faced mounting threats during the conflict.
QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio.
“This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy.
For Cheniere, the agreements secure another major long-term customer for its U.S. Gulf Coast operations.
The company currently operates approximately 56 MTPA of LNG production capacity across Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with another 5 MTPA under construction. One million tonnes annually under the new Sabine Pass agreement remains contingent on a final investment decision for the first phase of the terminal’s planned expansion.
The deal highlights QatarEnergy’s growing role not only as a major LNG producer but also as an international LNG trader, while adding another long-term source of U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that can reach global markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

high_priority_articles.title: South Sudan, Ethiopia and Rwanda rank among world's fastest-growing economies in 2026, outpacing Nigeria, South Africa, China and the US - Business Insider Africa
high_priority_articles.summary: South Sudan, Ethiopia and Rwanda rank among world's fastest-growing economies in 2026, outpacing Nigeria, South Africa, China and the US  Business Insider Africa
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- South Sudan's growth is driven by the recovery of its oil industry, while Ethiopia benefits from economic reforms and Rwanda from investments in construction, services, and tourism.
- Sub-Saharan Africa as a region is projected to outpace global economic growth, with an average of 4.5% in 2026 and 2027, compared to the global average of 3.1%.
- Rapid GDP growth percentages do not equate to economic size or wealth, and sustaining momentum will require diversification, increased investment, and improvements in household incomes.
According to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook, South Sudan leads Africa with projected real GDP growth of 10.5%, followed by Ethiopia at 9.2% and Rwanda at 7.4%.
The three countries occupy third, fourth and eighth positions, respectively, in a ranking of 18 selected fast-growing economies, reflecting different economic developments, from recovering oil production in South Sudan to reforms in Ethiopia and investment-led expansion in Rwanda.
Eight African countries feature in the ranking, highlighting the continent's growth potential despite persistent financial and political challenges.
What is driving growth in Africa's top three economies?
South Sudan's position largely reflects the recovery of its oil industry, which accounts for about 95% of exports and between 70% and 80% of government revenue.
The country's economy suffered a severe setback after fighting in neighbouring Sudan disrupted a pipeline carrying its crude oil to international markets.
According to the African Development Bank, South Sudan's GDP contracted by 27.6% in the 2023/24 financial year as oil production and exports collapsed.
With shipments recovering, the IMF expects economic output to rebound sharply, restoring some government revenue and foreign exchange earnings. However, much of this expansion represents a recovery from previous losses rather than growth across several industries.
South Sudan's heavy reliance on oil also leaves it vulnerable to renewed conflict, disruptions to export infrastructure and fluctuations in global petroleum prices.
Ethiopia's growth, meanwhile, follows a different path, supported by economic reforms, stronger exports, infrastructure development and expanding private-sector activity.
In July 2024, the government allowed the Ethiopian birr to trade more freely, introduced monetary policy reforms and secured IMF support as part of efforts to address foreign exchange shortages and restore economic stability.
These reforms have helped improve access to foreign currency, while coffee and gold exports have strengthened the country's foreign exchange earnings. Ethiopia has also opened sectors including banking and trade to greater foreign investment.
Despite these developments, inflation, external debt obligations and higher import costs continue to threaten household purchasing power and economic stability.
Rwanda's expansion is driven by construction, services, tourism and infrastructure investment as the country strengthens its position as a regional business destination.
According to the IMF, Rwanda's economy expanded by 9.7% in the first half of 2026, while stronger exports and remittance inflows helped narrow its external financing gap.
However, inflation reached 15.7% in August, reflecting domestic price pressures and higher international energy and fertiliser costs. Rwanda is also pursuing an IMF-supported financing programme to strengthen economic stability.
How Africa's fastest-growing economies compare with global powers
The IMF projects Nigeria's economy to expand by 4.2% in 2026, compared with 5.1% for Egypt and 1.0% for South Africa. South Sudan's projected growth is therefore more than twice Nigeria's rate and over ten times South Africa's.
Similarly, South Sudan, Ethiopia and Rwanda are expected to outperform major global economies, including China at 4.5%, the United States at 2.3% and the United Kingdom at 1.3%.
However, Guyana leads the global ranking with projected growth of 22.3%, largely driven by offshore oil production, followed by Taiwan at 10.7%, Vietnam at 8.4% and India at 7.0%.
Other African countries among the 18 selected fast-growing economies include Guinea at 7.2%, Benin, Niger and Sudan at 7.0% each, and Uganda at 6.2%.
Despite their higher growth rates, South Sudan, Ethiopia and Rwanda have much smaller economies than Nigeria, South Africa, China and the United States, highlighting the difference between rapid economic expansion and overall economic size.
For the three countries, sustaining growth will depend on attracting investment, creating jobs, diversifying production and improving household incomes.

Beyond Diplomacy: How Tanzanians in Korea are building bridges of opportunity
TANZANIA: WHEN Tanzanians across Korea gather in the coastal city of Yeosu on 24 and 25 October this year, they will be celebrating more than a national occasion abroad. They will be marking 34 years of friendship between Tanzania and the Republic of Korea and showing how much of that friendship now rests on people, not just on governments.
Tanzania Diaspora Day 2026 will bring together Tanzanians living in Korea, representatives of government institutions, invited guests and friends of Tanzania in Yeosu, Jeollanam-do. Alongside culture, sport and community, the two-day event poses a forward-looking question: how can the growing Tanzanian community in Korea help open a new chapter of cooperation in education, employment, innovation, trade and investment?
The Embassy has organised the event with the Association of Tanzanians in Korea (TANROK) in recognition of the diaspora’s contribution to Tanzania’s development through remittances, investment, skills transfer and entrepreneurship. In 2024, remittances reached 2.116 tr/-, while diaspora investment through UTT-AMIS funds rose to 7.5 bn/-, up from 6.4 bn/- in 2023. With the right policies and support, that contribution can grow further.
Three Decades of Friendship
Since the establishment of diplomatic relations in April 1992, Tanzania and Korea have built strong ties based on mutual respect and shared development goals. Cooperation now spans infrastructure, education, healthcare, technology, trade, investment, tourism and culture.
Momentum grew in June 2024, when Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of the United Republic of Tanzania, visited Korea for the inaugural Korea–Africa Summit. Among the outcomes was a framework providing up to USD 2.5 billion in concessional financing through Korea’s Economic Development Cooperation Fund (EDCF) for 2024–2028.
Yet people remain at the heart of the relationship. Tanzanian students at Korean universities, public officials on capacity-building programmes, researchers and entrepreneurs all strengthen ties in ways formal diplomacy cannot. Their friendships and networks bring our two societies closer, and Diaspora Day is a chance to celebrate them.
Yeosu Comes Alive
Yeosu, with its maritime heritage and international outlook, is a fitting host for a celebration of connections across borders. Alongside cultural performances celebrating the heritage of Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, the programme will feature information clinics connecting the Tanzanian diaspora with public and private Tanzanian institutions and service providers on immigration, taxation, ports and logistics, banking and investment. There will also be room for open dialogue between the Embassy and the diaspora on welfare, careers, business and continued engagement with home.
Sport will also feature prominently, with planned friendly matches between Tanzanian participants, neighbouring African diaspora communities and youth teams. The highlight will be a match between Tanzania’s Under-17 national team, the Serengeti Boys, and Yeosu Marine FC U-18, a reminder that sport is a universal language that brings people together.
The Diaspora as a Bridge
The Tanzanian community in Korea, estimated at around 400 people and comprising students, researchers, professionals, entrepreneurs and families, is an important asset for both countries. Because they understand both societies, diaspora members are well placed to link businesses, universities, research institutions and communities.
They can introduce Korean investors to opportunities in Tanzania, promote Tanzanian products and tourist destinations, support academic exchanges and build partnerships in technology and entrepreneurship. Their knowledge of Korea’s business environment can also feed back into Tanzania’s development through mentorship, knowledge transfer and investment.
That is why we see the diaspora not merely as citizens living abroad, but as partners in economic diplomacy. The Embassy is committed to deepening engagement with Tanzanians in Korea, improving access to information and backing initiatives that connect their expertise with opportunities at home.
Just as important are the everyday encounters in classrooms, workplaces and neighbourhoods, where Tanzanians introduce their culture and aspirations to Korean society. These people-to-people ties are the foundation on which diplomatic and economic partnerships grow and prosper.
From Scholarships to Skills
Education has long been at the core of Tanzania–Korea cooperation. Through the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), Korean universities and other institutions, Tanzanian students, officials, researchers and professionals have benefited from scholarships, postgraduate study and technical training.
Korea’s support also reaches infrastructure, healthcare and institutional capacity-building. According to Tanzania’s Ministry of Finance, KOICA had provided approximately USD 139.5 million in grants under a cooperation programme established in 2014, as reported in March 2024. The EDCF, meanwhile, finances major development projects under the USD 2.5 billion framework.
The lasting value lies beyond the numbers, in the knowledge, expertise and networks these programmes create. Tanzanian beneficiaries gain exposure to advanced technologies and to Korea’s own experience of industrial transformation.
As we celebrate Diaspora Day, we extend heartfelt appreciation to KOICA, Korean universities and other development partners for their contribution to building Tanzania’s human capital. The next step is to link scholarships and training more closely with research, innovation, industry and skilled employment, so that both nations continue to benefit. In this regard, Tanzania commends the Korean government’s decision to extend the D-10 job-seeker visa for graduates of Korean universities from two years to a maximum of three.
Connecting Talent with Opportunity
Skilled employment is a promising new frontier. Korea’s ageing population and labour shortages in some industries have raised demand for international talent, while Tanzania has a growing pool of skilled professionals in engineering, information technology, healthcare, research, digital services and technical trades.
During President Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan’s 2024 visit, Tanzania expressed interest in labour cooperation through Korea’s Employment Permit System (EPS). Building on this, the two countries could pursue structured dialogue on professional visas, skills recognition, Korean-language training and partnerships between employers, universities and technical institutions, in line with Korea’s immigration and labour regulations.
Such cooperation should do more than fill vacancies. Korean employers would gain qualified professionals; Tanzanian workers would gain international experience and expertise that benefit their careers and their country. Any arrangement must be guided by verified labourmarket demand, transparent recruitment, fair working conditions and strong protection of workers’ rights.

Empowering the Next Generation
Young people must be at the centre of this agenda. Tanzanian graduates and professionals need the skills, language proficiency and practical experience to compete in Korea’s evolving labour market. Partnerships among universities, research institutions, training centres and businesses could open doors to internships, exchanges and joint research, within safe, transparent and lawful pathways.
The diaspora can help through mentorship, networking and support for newly arriving students and professionals. The Embassy, working with Tanzanian and Korean institutions, will continue to build practical partnerships that help young people realise their potential.
Looking Ahead
Diaspora Day 2026 will be more than a celebration of identity, culture and community. It is a platform to strengthen connections, engage with institutions from home, recognise Korea’s longstanding contribution to Tanzania’s development and explore how 34 years of friendship can inspire new partnerships in innovation, skills and employment.
I look forward to joining our diaspora community in Yeosu. I encourage every Tanzanian in Korea to take part, celebrate our shared heritage, strengthen their networks and find ways to contribute to Tanzania’s development.
I equally invite Korean institutions, universities, businesses, employers and development partners to keep building meaningful partnerships with Tanzania.
Tanzania–Korea relations will be strengthened by our people, enriched by our cultures and sustained by the opportunities we create together for future generations. Let us each play our part.
