high_priority_articles.title: Europe’s Midterm Calculation: Why a Weakened Trump Means a Harder Line on NATO - Modern Diplomacy
high_priority_articles.summary: Europe’s Midterm Calculation: Why a Weakened Trump Means a Harder Line on NATO  Modern Diplomacy
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Four Options, Three Days Later
On 6 November, three days after Americans vote, Pentagon officials are due to put at least four courses of action for America’s military footprint in Europe in front of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. They are the product of a posture review that Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s policy chief, says is meant to move NATO “fast and irreversibly” toward Europe taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defence — and of a questionnaire asking allies whether they restricted US use of their bases and airspace during the Iran war. A Pentagon official has already spoken of “clearly at least some demand signal” for options that downgrade US forces. Many in European capitals read the timing as lucky: a president humbled at the ballot box, the reasoning goes, will be in no position to gut the alliance. That reading is backwards. A weakened Trump is likely to be a harder one on NATO.
A President Losing Altitude — and an Alliance Already Sorted
The numbers are bleak for the White House. A Reuters/Ipsos poll put Trump’s approval at 31% on 19 October, the lowest of his career, with Democrats 12 points ahead on the generic ballot. Decision Desk HQ’s model gives Democrats a 78% chance of taking the House and 57% of taking the Senate. The main drag is the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on 28 February, which pushed diesel to a record $6.52 a gallon in September.
The war has also become the organising grievance of Trump’s NATO policy. When European allies declined to help secure the Strait of Hormuz in the spring, Trump openly mused about leaving the alliance. Since then the Pentagon has cancelled an armoured brigade rotation to Poland and announced up to 5,000 troop cuts, mainly in Germany, and convened a “Bergen Group” of favoured allies — Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Finland — that pointedly excludes Britain, France and the Baltic states. Congress has drawn lines of its own: a 2023 law bars withdrawal from NATO without Senate or congressional approval, and the 2026 defence bill forbids cutting US forces in Europe below 76,000 without first consulting allies.
Congress Guards the Floor, Not the Ceiling
The case for optimism is intuitive. A Democratic House would control spending, wield subpoena power and hold a veto over the annual defence bill, and Republican senators already restive over Iran would feel freer to break ranks. Some of that is true. But it confuses two different things Congress can protect.
What Congress can legislate is the floor of the alliance: formal membership, troop numbers, the rule that an American general commands NATO forces in Europe. What it cannot legislate is the ceiling — the credibility of the American promise to fight. Deterrence under Article 5, NATO’s mutual-defence clause, lives in the Kremlin’s assessment of the president, not of the appropriations committee. A Trump who keeps 76,001 troops in Europe while telling a campaign rally, as he did on 20 October, that “we will have no choice but to leave” if allies do not “find their way” has complied with every statute while hollowing out the thing the statutes exist to protect.
More important is the direction in which domestic pressure has already pushed him. The clearest test came on 9 October. Facing record fuel prices four weeks before the vote, Trump struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for millions of tonnes of Russian diesel; the Treasury exempted cargoes from sanctions until April 2027 — the longest diesel waiver since 2022, and one that cut against a Russia sanctions law Trump had signed a month earlier. Electoral weakness did not make him more deferential to allies or to Congress. It made him willing to hand Moscow a concession, over Ukrainian and European objections, to move a domestic number.
The Bergen Group follows the same logic. Allies are now sorted by loyalty as much as by capability. The Pentagon’s questionnaire asks whether governments publicly back US foreign policy, and Politico reported that the administration had weighed a “naughty and nice list”. Analysts quoted by Euronews link Britain and France’s exclusion to their initial refusal to join the Iran war, and the Baltics’ to their rejection of Colby’s advice to soften their tone towards Moscow. This is not an incoherent policy waiting to be corrected. It is a coherent one — NATO as a tiered clientele — and it needs no congressional consent to function.
Trump’s own record points the same way. Six weeks after losing the House in 2018, he announced a withdrawal from Syria over his defence secretary’s objections; Jim Mattis resigned the next day. The New York Times later reported that Trump had repeatedly told aides that year he wanted to leave NATO. Presidents who lose leverage at home turn to the arena where they act alone. Trump, whose foreign policy already runs on executive orders, sanctions licences and phone calls, has less to lose from a hostile Congress than any modern predecessor. As a recent Modern Diplomacy analysis put it, a defeated president becomes hurried rather than cautious.
The strongest objection is that the Republican coalition is already cracking on precisely these issues. Mitch McConnell publicly rebuked Trump’s NATO threats in April; four Republican senators voted in September to end the Iran war; farm-state Republicans forced a reversal on diesel exports. A bad night on 3 November would speed this up, and a party turning towards 2028 may want distance from an unpopular president’s feuds with allies.
The dynamic is real, but it buys less than it appears. Several of the loudest dissenters, McConnell and Thom Tillis among them, are retiring. The September war-powers resolution still failed 50–49 — the twentieth attempt. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, a margin no forecast offers. Defections limit what Trump can get Congress to do; they barely touch what he can do without it.
So Europe does gain room — in Washington’s legislature rather than its executive, and only briefly. The 2027 defence bill passed the House 216–212 in July but stalled in the Senate, so it will almost certainly be finished in the “lame-duck” session between the election and January. The House version would extend the 76,000-troop floor, order a review of whether the 5,000-troop cut broke last year’s law, and force the Pentagon to justify its posture decisions. That is where European diplomatic energy belongs this winter.
Three Ways the Winter Could Go
Base case — the same policy, delivered harder (55%). Democrats take the House and possibly the Senate. Trump reads the result as proof of disloyalty from allies who “weren’t there”, not as a mandate for moderation. The posture review produces cuts that keep US forces just above the 76,000 floor; Bergen-style sorting widens, with Denmark — fresh from a Greenland basing deal — reportedly next in line; Russia policy keeps bending to fuel prices. There is no formal exit, only steady erosion of credibility. The key assumption: Trump stays inside the legal guardrails while probing their edges.
Downside — the guardrails get tested (25%). The Iran war widens — Washington has already ordered most embassy staff out of Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks — and the Pentagon cites operational necessity to pull air defences, munitions and support units out of Europe faster than the consultation rules allow, daring a new Democratic House to litigate. The damage is less numerical than political: Europe learns that the floor itself is negotiable. For governments and companies exposed to NATO’s eastern flank, this is the scenario least priced in.
Upside — Congress locks the floor in place (20%). A chastened Republican Senate leadership and a Democratic House use the lame-duck defence bill to entrench Europe’s posture; Hegseth picks the mildest of his four options; Trump’s attention moves to an Iran settlement and the December G20 summit in Miami, to which he has invited Putin. Europe gets a calmer 2027 — but on borrowed time, because the shift towards Colby’s “NATO 3.0” continues regardless.
Prepare for the Same Policy, Only Harder
Europe’s midterm calculation should not turn on whether Trump will be weaker after 3 November. He almost certainly will be. The question is where that weakness shows. It will show in Congress. It will not show in the policy that matters most to Europe, which runs through the Oval Office, the Pentagon’s posture review and the president’s phone line to Moscow. Governments that spend the winter waiting for a chastened president will be surprised; those that spend it working the lame-duck Congress and speeding up their own rearmament will not.
The signal to watch is the final text of the 2027 defence bill in December: does it extend the 76,000-troop floor and attach conditions to whichever option Hegseth picks? If it does, Europe has bought time. If it does not, the floor was always a courtesy. Either way, NATO’s next chapter will be written by a president with less to lose than ever.

high_priority_articles.title: Burnham warned ‘Britain is at risk’ as a damning NATO ranking exposes UK’s military readiness crisis - London Business News
high_priority_articles.summary: Burnham warned ‘Britain is at risk’ as a damning NATO ranking exposes UK’s military readiness crisis  London Business News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Defence Committee warns military readiness must improve before 2030, as Kemi Badenoch accuses the government of delaying crucial spending decisions and leaving Britain exposed to growing security risks.
Britain has been ranked second from bottom among NATO allies on an internal measure of how effectively members are meeting their rearmament commitments, raising fresh questions about the country’s ability to prepare for a potential Russian attack on the alliance before the end of the decade.
A report by the House of Commons Defence Committee places the UK 31st out of 32 NATO countries, with only Iceland — which has no military capability — ranked lower. The findings expose a gap between the government’s defence ambitions and the readiness of the armed forces, despite plans to invest almost £300bn over the next four years.
With British intelligence and other NATO assessments indicating that Russia could attack the alliance as soon as 2030, the committee warned that the timetable for addressing military weaknesses was becoming increasingly urgent.
“And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough,” said Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the committee.
Read more related news:
https://londonlovesbusiness.com/wp-admin/post.php?post=240497&action=edit&wpil_reminder_notice=CnBP6FheXjfZhdPZB7nAWRPIrgv9ViaJ
The report described Britain’s position as stark. “According to an internal document apparently drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, the UK is number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries,” it said.
The ranking intensifies scrutiny of whether the government’s planned spending increases will translate into forces capable of responding quickly to a crisis. Defence investment can fund new equipment, but deterrence also depends on existing ships, aircraft and other military assets being available, maintained and ready for deployment.
Ed Arnold, senior research fellow for European security at the Royal United Services Institute, told the committee that Britain’s position was “pretty poor”.
“The only way that you can increase that really is through cash because it’s all about fleet availability, it’s all about readiness to be out of the door as soon as possible and as soon as needed,” he said.
The government’s Defence Investment Plan, published in June, commits £298bn over the four years to 2029-30, with the aim of raising defence spending to 2.7 per cent of national income. A longer-term NATO commitment envisages Britain and its allies spending 3.5 per cent of national income on defence by 2035.
But the gap between those targets has become a source of political friction, with the Conservatives accusing ministers of postponing difficult decisions while warning that the security environment is deteriorating.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has called on the government to find additional money for defence in next week’s Budget, arguing that the necessary funding should be prioritised through welfare cuts and tighter control of borrowing.
“If, at this Budget, he does not find the money to get to 3%, John Healey has an awful lot of explaining to do,” she said in a speech in Westminster.
Badenoch described the delay in setting out a clear path towards higher defence spending as “unconscionable”, criticising reports that the decision had been deferred to a spending review that itself had been pushed back until next autumn.
She argued that the additional funding required to reach 3 per cent of gross domestic product by 2030 was “less than a third of the increase in welfare since Labour came to office”, framing the dispute as a question of government priorities rather than affordability alone.
“Britain is at risk,” she said. “John Healey said so himself, and no amount of political difficulty should prevent us from responding to that risk.”
Healey has argued that Britain must commit to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030. The government is not expected to set out a full route towards NATO’s longer-term 3.5 per cent target until next year’s spending review, leaving uncertainty over the scale and timing of future funding.
The debate is particularly pressing for the Royal Navy, whose ability to operate in the High North is central to plans to deter Russian threats across the North Atlantic and surrounding waters.
The government is investing in its Hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion concepts, but the Defence Committee warned that the service’s current equipment readiness and platform numbers were substantially below its stated requirements.
“Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements,” the report said.
With 2030 identified as a key date for Britain to be ready to deter or defeat a Russian threat, the committee called for “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the armed forces in the High North.
The Ministry of Defence told the inquiry that equipment was maintained at different levels of readiness according to operational requirements. Military platforms move through cycles of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, with their readiness determined in part by the NATO capabilities they are expected to provide.
That distinction matters. A spending commitment is not the same as an operational capability, and a new platform offers limited immediate reassurance if existing equipment cannot be deployed when required.
The committee concluded that the near-£300bn investment programme was the bedrock of Britain’s contribution to deterring or defeating Russian aggression from 2030. But it also made clear that new procurement alone would not be enough: ministers must improve the readiness of the forces already in service.
The government now faces a difficult choice over how quickly to increase defence spending while balancing public services, welfare commitments and the cost of servicing national debt. The Conservatives are pressing for a faster commitment, while ministers must determine how to finance higher spending and convert it into military capability.
For Britain, the central question is whether its armed forces can become sufficiently equipped and ready before the strategic deadline identified by its own government. With the country near the bottom of NATO’s internal rearmament table, the committee’s warning is that the time available to close the gap is running short.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea Built the Power Plants but Has No Lines to Carry the Electricity: 3.1 Trillion Won in Compensation, Yongin Semiconductor Grid Just 1% Complete - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea Built the Power Plants but Has No Lines to Carry the Electricity: 3.1 Trillion Won in Compensation, Yongin Semiconductor Grid Just 1% Complete  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Power plants have been built, but with no transmission lines to carry the electricity, facilities that halted operations have received more than 3 trillion won in compensation over the past five years. For the same reason, dedicated transmission grids for South Korea's core national industrial complexes remain in the single digits in completion rates, raising fears of power supply disruptions even for the Yongin semiconductor cluster, which aims to begin operations in 2027.
According to the National Assembly Budget Office's report "2026 Status and Issues of Public Institutions," 112,430 GWh of electricity could not be generated from 2021 through the first half of this year due to transmission constraints. Korea Electric Power Corporation paid power producers a total of 3.1651 trillion won (approximately $2.4 billion) over the period in Expected Profit Settlement (MAP) payments for electricity they failed to generate. These are compensation-type payments made regardless of whether a generator is running.
Currently, 12 power plants nationwide are having their output curtailed due to transmission equipment problems. The Taean Thermal Power Plant in South Chungcheong Province had to forgo 43,590 GWh—24.9% of its planned generation—from 2021 through June of this year. Seven plants in the Gangwon region also absorbed a 22,310 GWh reduction in output over five and a half years.
The root of the problem is the construction speed gap between generating facilities and transmission networks. Solar and other renewable facilities are completed in 1 to 3 years, thermal power plants in 5 to 7 years, and nuclear plants in 7 to 9 years, but large-capacity 345 kV transmission lines take an average of 9 to 13 years to finish, including site selection and mediation of resident disputes.
The 500 kV high-voltage direct current (HVDC) project to send large-scale power from the East Coast to the Seoul metropolitan area has made no progress, as Hanam City has refused to expand the East Seoul converter station, insisting that permits cannot be granted without resident consent. The 345 kV Dangjin Thermal Power Plant–Sinseokmun–Sinsongsan line has also been delayed by 7 years and 6 months, from its original June 2021 completion date to 2028, as resident opposition over electromagnetic field concerns dragged on.
The compensation Korea Electric Power Corporation pays without actually receiving electricity is reflected in power purchase costs, pushing up the overall cost base for electricity rates. The cost of mismatched infrastructure ultimately lands on consumers.
The supply-side bottleneck is even more acute for dedicated grids serving industrial complexes that consume large amounts of power. The Yongin Advanced System Semiconductor Cluster, which aims to be the world's largest single semiconductor base, is a prime example. The government and industry have set the start of operations for SK Hynix's general industrial complex at 2027 and Samsung Electronics' national industrial complex at 2029, on the premise of early operation.
However, the Yongin transmission project, which involves building 14 345 kV lines, had spent only 19.4 billion won (approximately $14.6 million) of its 3.7 trillion won (approximately $2.8 billion) total project cost as of the end of 2025—a completion rate of 1%. Under the annual spending plan, only 49.7 billion won (approximately $37.5 million) is scheduled to be spent from 2026 to 2029, while 3.6451 trillion won (approximately $2.8 billion), or 98.6% of the remaining project cost, is concentrated after 2030. In effect, little real progress can be expected over the next four years.

|---|---|---|---|
| Project | Total Project Cost | Spending as of End-2025 (Completion Rate) | Completion/Operation Target | 
| Yongin Semiconductor Cluster | 3.7 trillion won (approximately $2.8 billion) | 19.4 billion won (approximately $14.6 million) (1%) | Completion Dec. 2036 / Operations 2027–2029 | 
| Songdo Bio Cluster | 330 billion won (approximately $249.0 million) | 65 billion won (approximately $49.0 million) (20%) | December 2028 | 
| Yeosu National Industrial Complex | 8.4 billion won (approximately $6.3 million) | 7 million won (approximately $5,300) (5%) | September 2030 | 
Note: Based on the National Assembly Budget Office report "2026 Status and Issues of Public Institutions"
Other key industrial complexes are in similar shape. The Yeosu National Industrial Complex transmission project, targeting completion in September 2030, has spent just 7 million won (approximately $5,300), barely clearing a 5% completion rate. The Songdo Bio Cluster project, aiming for completion in December 2028, remains at 20% of its planned 330 billion won (approximately $249.0 million) investment. Although the government has introduced a special law to shorten the overall construction period to nine years, with only two to four years left and work still in its early stages, analysts say on-time completion is effectively impossible.
Experts say the practice of pursuing generation and transmission separately needs to be overhauled. The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), under the U.S. Department of Energy, has advised a proactive approach that identifies areas needing transmission in advance and incorporates them into construction plans. Some also argue that, given a supply-demand structure in which production and consumption areas are widely separated, South Korea should urgently build a system that generates energy directly in consumption areas.
The National Assembly Budget Office noted that with work still in its early stages, supply may fail to arrive when power demand materializes. It warned that delayed grid expansion could trigger generation constraints and settlement costs again, and that the progress and spending plans of projects serving major demand centers must be monitored so the gap with demand timing does not widen. Korea Electric Power Corporation said all relevant agencies will cooperate to supply power to national industrial complexes without schedule disruptions.
The issue directly affects investment schedules in semiconductors, petrochemicals, bio and other core national industries. Even after a factory is completed and equipment is installed, mass production can be pushed back if power is not connected, while on the generation side, accumulating compensation feeds back into cost pressure on electricity rates. Analysts say that unless grid construction starts, permitting and mediation of resident disputes are managed under a single timetable, the lag between equipment investment and infrastructure investment could erode industrial competitiveness.

high_priority_articles.title: Professor Kim Jung-ho: "South Korea's Chip Success Wasn't Just Technology—It Was a Windfall… HBM Was Decisive" - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: Professor Kim Jung-ho: "South Korea's Chip Success Wasn't Just Technology—It Was a Windfall… HBM Was Decisive"  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
An analysis has emerged that unexpected external factors, alongside technological prowess, played a decisive role in the growth of South Korea's semiconductor industry. Kim Jung-ho, a distinguished professor at Yonsei University, said in a recent appearance on a YouTube channel that the flagship businesses of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rode the AI boom into a heyday that diverged from their original plans.
Kim explained that while Samsung Electronics set its sights on becoming the world's No. 1 in system semiconductors, its market share actually declined, whereas DRAM—its traditional mainstay—enjoyed an unexpected boom as the AI industry grew. "DRAM, which no one had even considered, hit the jackpot," he said. "We thought the DRAM era was over and shifted our investment direction, but the opportunity came in that very process." He added, "It's less that South Korea pulled it off and more that a windfall came rushing in."
SK Hynix's investment in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) was cited as another key case. HBM is memory that stacks multiple DRAM chips vertically to boost data processing speed and efficiency, and it is essential for AI chips that require large-scale computation. Kim noted that SK Hynix continued developing HBM even while it was struggling financially.
Initially, HBM did not win much traction in the gaming PC market. But the situation changed as the AI industry surged with the arrival of ChatGPT. Data centers running AI services needed high-performance graphics processing units (GPUs), and demand surged for high-performance memory to support GPU computing speeds. "No one knew ChatGPT would succeed like this," Kim said, explaining that HBM resolves the bottleneck in which "GPUs run fast but memory can't keep up."
He predicted that new opportunities could open up for South Korea's battery industry as well. In the electric vehicle battery market, Chinese companies hold sway with mass production and price competitiveness, but a different competitive landscape could take shape in physical AI fields such as robotics, according to his analysis. Human-sized robots have limited space to house batteries, making high energy density critical. "Batteries for physical AI have to be small, so quality has to be high," Kim said. "That's why South Korean batteries are at an advantage."
He paid particular attention to solid-state batteries. Solid-state batteries, which can address the limitations of conventional liquid-electrolyte batteries, are considered a next-generation battery technology. He said South Korea and Japan are strong contenders in the race to commercialize solid-state batteries, and called attention to South Korean companies' development of related technology.
Kim named defense and AI as the industries to watch after semiconductors. In particular, he stressed the need to foster an industry that combines AI with drones to boost defense efficiency. "If we're thinking about the next defense industry, I'd say drones or AI," he said. "We need to build an industry that uses existing AI to defend South Korea sufficiently." He also stressed the importance of overhauling the education system for the AI era. "We need to shift to an education that properly uses AI to produce people who become masters of AI," he said.
Meanwhile, at the "Smart Energy Plus (SEP) 2026" conference, to be held on the 29th at COEX in Gangnam District, Seoul, senior executives from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix will take the stage to discuss the future of AI and semiconductors. Han Jae-jun, a master (managing director) at Samsung Electronics' AX/PI Center, will present a strategy for integrating AI from design through production to raise development speed and manufacturing productivity. Samsung Electronics will also disclose a case in which it used reinforcement learning and genetic algorithms to automate repetitive tasks such as transistor sizing and to predict potential design-rule violations in advance, cutting design time by about 50%.
Choi Jun-yong, vice president of HBM business planning at SK Hynix, will address the shift of the bottleneck limiting performance gains from computing to memory and then to power, under the theme "Memory That Defines the Future of AI." Just as growth in devices drove demand in the past, in the AI era the "growth of intelligence" will expand the market, according to his argument. The next challenge is the "Energy Wall" arising from surging data center power consumption. SK Hynix proposes as solutions raising HBM's bandwidth per watt, reducing the distance between computing units and memory through 3D stacking, and architectures optimized for workloads such as customized HBM.
Kim's analysis shows that South Korea's semiconductor success is the product of technological prowess and coincidence combined. The implication is that investment decisions should not rest solely on the "planned success" of a particular technology, but should also examine how the unpredictable expansion of the AI industry is reshaping the structure of memory demand. In addition, which positions South Korean companies secure in next-generation fields such as physical AI, solid-state batteries and defense will be key to the next growth cycle.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korean economy's growth likely picked up in Q3 on chip exports: Reuters poll - Central Oregon Daily
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korean economy's growth likely picked up in Q3 on chip exports: Reuters poll  Central Oregon Daily
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Renusri K
BENGALURU, Oct 23 (Reuters) - South Korea's economy grew slightly faster in the third quarter than in April to June, as booming semiconductor exports and AI-related investment helped offset still-uneven domestic demand, a Reuters poll of economists showed.
An AI-fuelled chip boom has supported South Korea's economy for years, but has also made it increasingly reliant on chip exports, with the gains yet to spread widely through the domestic economy. Meanwhile, high borrowing costs and elevated household debt have weighed on household consumption.
Exports rose 84% from a year earlier to a record $120.9 billion in September, led by a 262.8% surge in chip exports to $60.3 billion. Semiconductors accounted for nearly half of total shipments, underlining the industry's outsized role in driving gross domestic product growth.
The economy grew a seasonally adjusted 0.7% in the July-September quarter, according to the median forecast of 16 economists polled from October 14-23, a slight pickup from 0.6% growth in the April-June quarter. Forecasts ranged from 0.5% to 1.6%.
"The question is whether we will see benefits from the export sector. It is important to see the transmission to the domestic economy, and one of the key channels is fiscal policy to ease the pressures," said Jeong Woo Park, Asia economist at Nomura.
"Financial conditions are becoming less accommodative and the labour market is structurally in downturn. With companies adopting AI more rapidly, for the younger generation it is very hard to find jobs," Park said.
The contrast between the fast-growing chip sector and softer demand elsewhere in the economy has raised concerns among some economists that the recovery, which began in the first quarter, is becoming increasingly uneven.
On a year-on-year basis, GDP was forecast to grow 3.0%, slowing from 3.7% in the previous quarter, based on the median estimate from 16 economists.
"The concentration risk of growth being driven by AI should worry the BOK to some extent, but I don't think they are showing it too much," said Kelvin Lam, senior economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "The Korean economy is very vulnerable to this as everything now is driven mainly by the semiconductor industry."
The Bank of Korea held its benchmark interest rate at 3.00% on Thursday, in line with consensus expectations, and raised its growth forecast to 3.3% for this year and 2.9% for next year.
A separate Reuters poll forecast growth of 3.5% in 2026.
(Reporting by Renusri K; Polling by Pranoy Krishna and Rahul Trivedi in Bengaluru and Jihoon Lee in Seoul; Editing by Vivek Mishra, Hari Kishan)

By Steve Holland and Ryan Patrick Jones
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which will begin next Thursday, the White House said on Friday.
The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defence Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on Tuesday to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," a White House statement said.
Ukraine's top negotiator, David Arakhamia, said on Telegram that the humanitarian operation would start once a ceasefire was in place.
He said the accord, the result of a long process involving Melania Trump and Pope Leo, would set up a humanitarian corridor for residents to leave and allow assistance into the town.
In Moscow, the Kremlin welcomed the agreement. It praised Melania Trump's role in securing the agreement and said President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin had discussed details.
The Kremlin said earlier this week that work was under way to ease the humanitarian situation in Oleshky after Putin told the pope he was ready to cooperate on the issue.
The development comes as President Trump pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to reach an agreement with Putin to end the war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
FIRST LADY HAS SOUGHT TO HELP UKRAINIAN CHILDREN
Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," Melania Trump said in the statement.
The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from both countries to visit residents in their homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed American media organization accompanying the teams to document the process, the first lady said.
Newsmax, a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted "exclusive access to document the effort."
Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people — primarily elderly residents, along with about 50 children — down from roughly 24,000 before the war, the White House said. About 90% of the city was flooded following the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House.
The statement said Melania Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
(Reporting by Steve Holland and Susan Heavey; Writing by Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto; Editing by Katharine Jackson, David Ljunggren, Caitlin Webber, Rod Nickel and Ron Popeski)
